title: Activation Functions – The Magic Spark ⚡
description: Discover how activations introduce non‑linearity and which one to choose.

slides.title: Why Not Just Linear? 📈
slides.content:
# Without Non‑Linearity, Layers Collapse

If you stack multiple Dense layers without activation, the entire network is equivalent to a single linear transformation.

Activation functions introduce **non‑linearity**, allowing the network to learn complex patterns.

> Analogy: A chef mixing ingredients in a specific way (non‑linear) rather than just pouring them all into one pot (linear).

slides.title: Common Activation Functions 🎚️
slides.content:
# ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)
`f(x) = max(0, x)` – Fast, effective, default for hidden layers.

# Sigmoid
`f(x) = 1 / (1 + exp(-x))` – Squashes to (0,1). Good for binary output.

# Softmax
Exponentiates and normalises a vector into probabilities that sum to 1. Used for multi‑class output.

# Tanh
`f(x) = (exp(x)-exp(-x))/(exp(x)+exp(-x))` – Squashes to (-1,1).

quizData.question: Which activation is best for the output layer of a 10‑class classifier?
quizData.explanation: Softmax produces a probability distribution over the 10 classes.

slides.title: Activations in Practice
slides.content: You can apply activations in two ways:
slides.codeSnippet:
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense, Activation

# 1. As part of layer
model.add(Dense(64, activation='relu'))

# 2. As separate layer
model.add(Dense(64))
model.add(Activation('relu'))

slides.title: Dead ReLU Problem 💀
slides.content:
## ReLU Can Die

If a neuron always outputs 0, its gradient is zero and it stops learning. Use **LeakyReLU** or **ELU** as alternatives to mitigate this.

quizData.question: A network with only linear activations can approximate any function if it has enough layers.
quizData.explanation: Without non‑linearity, the whole network is linear, limited to linear functions.
